steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper showing that pretrained vision-language models like CLIP can be used as zero-shot reward models for reinforcement learning. Explain the reward specification problem, what earlier VLM-based approaches did, and walk through our four main contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Problem: reward specification for vision-based RL is costly
- Idea: pretrained VLMs as zero-shot, language-grounded reward models
- Contribution 1: VLM-RM method
- Contribution 2: classic control benchmarks
- Contribution 3: MuJoCo humanoid tasks
- Contribution 4: scaling with VLM size
- Outlook

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem
  - training RL agents on complex vision-based tasks is hard: reward specification costly
  - manual reward functions often infeasible for real world tasks; learning reward model from human feedback expensive
  - need more sample-efficient, natural way to specify rewards
- Idea
  - pretrained VLMs e.g. CLIP (cite), Flamingo (cite) -> reward signals from natural language
  - prior attempts: extensive fine-tuning of VLMs (cite) or complex ad-hoc reward extraction (cite)
  - we show simple techniques work as zero-shot language-grounded reward models if the model is capable enough; four contributions
- Contribution 1: VLM-RM (Section 3)
  - general method: pre-trained VLMs as reward model for vision-based RL
  - implementation: CLIP; reward = cos-similarity between CLIP embedding of current state and simple language prompt
  - optional regularization: "baseline prompt" for neutral state; partial projection onto baseline->target direction
- Contribution 2: CartPole and MountainCar (Section 4.2)
  - high correlation with ground truth rewards; policies trained successfully with CLIP reward
  - more realistic textures -> better CLIP reward model
- Contribution 3: MuJoCo humanoid (Figure 1; Section 4.3)
  - raising arms, lotus position, splits, kneeling
  - CLIP reward from single sentence prompts, e.g. "a humanoid robot kneeling"
- Contribution 4: scaling (Section 4.4)
  - VLM scale strongly correlated with VLM-RM quality
  - humanoid tasks only learned with largest publicly available CLIP model
- Outlook
  - VLMs are powerful zero-shot reward models
  - current models like CLIP have limitations, expected mostly overcome by larger, more capable VLMs
  - VLM-RMs likely enable training for increasingly sophisticated tasks from human-written descriptions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Training reinforcement learning (RL) agents for complex tasks in vision-based domains can be hard, because specifying the reward is costly. For real world tasks it is often not feasible to specify reward functions by hand, and learning a reward model from human feedback is usually expensive. If we want RL to be more useful in practical applications, we need to find a way to specify reward functions that is more sample-efficient and more natural.

A natural approach is to use pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), like CLIP and Flamingo, to give reward signals based on natural language. But previous attempts at using VLMs to provide rewards need a lot of fine-tuning of the VLMs or complicated ad-hoc procedures to get rewards out of the VLMs. In this work we show that simple techniques for using VLMs as zero-shot language-grounded reward models work well, as long as the underlying model we choose is capable enough. We make four key contributions.

First, we propose VLM-RM, a general method for using pre-trained VLMs as a reward model for vision-based RL tasks (Section 3). We give a concrete implementation which uses CLIP as the VLM, and the reward function is the cos-similarity between the CLIP embedding of the current environment state and a simple language prompt. Optionally, the reward model can be regularized by giving a "baseline prompt" that describes a neutral state of the environment and partially projecting the representations onto the direction between the baseline and target prompts when we compute the reward.

- Contribution 2: CartPole and MountainCar (Section 4.2): high correlation with ground truth rewards, policies solve tasks; realistic textures help
- Contribution 3: MuJoCo humanoid (Figure 1; Section 4.3): raising arms, lotus position, splits, kneeling; single sentence prompts, e.g. "a humanoid robot kneeling"
- Contribution 4: scaling (Section 4.4): VLM scale strongly correlated with VLM-RM quality; humanoid only with largest public CLIP
- Outlook: VLMs powerful zero-shot reward models; limitations expected to be overcome by larger VLMs; increasingly sophisticated tasks from human-written descriptions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Training reinforcement learning (RL) agents for complex tasks in vision-based domains can be hard, because specifying the reward is costly. For real world tasks it is often not feasible to specify reward functions by hand, and learning a reward model from human feedback is usually expensive. If we want RL to be more useful in practical applications, we need to find a way to specify reward functions that is more sample-efficient and more natural.

A natural approach is to use pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), like CLIP and Flamingo, to give reward signals based on natural language. But previous attempts at using VLMs to provide rewards need a lot of fine-tuning of the VLMs or complicated ad-hoc procedures to get rewards out of the VLMs. In this work we show that simple techniques for using VLMs as zero-shot language-grounded reward models work well, as long as the underlying model we choose is capable enough. We make four key contributions.

First, we propose VLM-RM, a general method for using pre-trained VLMs as a reward model for vision-based RL tasks (Section 3). We give a concrete implementation which uses CLIP as the VLM, and the reward function is the cos-similarity between the CLIP embedding of the current environment state and a simple language prompt. Optionally, the reward model can be regularized by giving a "baseline prompt" that describes a neutral state of the environment and partially projecting the representations onto the direction between the baseline and target prompts when we compute the reward.

Second, we validate the method in the standard CartPole and MountainCar RL benchmarks (Section 4.2). VLM-RMs are highly correlated with the ground truth rewards of the environments, and we are able to train policies that solve the tasks with CLIP as the reward model. We also find that CLIP works better as a reward model when the environment is rendered with more realistic textures.

Third, we train a MuJoCo humanoid to learn complex tasks like raising its arms, sitting in a lotus position, doing the splits, and kneeling (Figure 1; Section 4.3), with a CLIP reward model that comes from single sentence text prompts (e.g., "a humanoid robot kneeling").

Fourth, we look at how the performance of VLM-RMs scales with the size of the VLM, and we find that VLM scale is strongly correlated with VLM-RM quality (Section 4.4). In particular, we can only learn the humanoid tasks in Figure 1 with the largest publicly available CLIP model.

Our results show that VLMs are powerful zero-shot reward models. Current models such as CLIP have important limitations that are still there when they are used as VLM-RMs, but we expect these limitations to be mostly overcome when larger and more capable VLMs become available. Overall, VLM-RMs will likely let us train models to do more and more sophisticated tasks from task descriptions written by humans.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Training reinforcement learning (RL) agents to perform complex tasks in vision-based domains can be difficult, because of the high costs associated with reward specification. Manually specifying reward functions for real world tasks is often infeasible, and learning a reward model from human feedback is typically expensive. To make RL more useful in practical applications, it is critical to find a more sample-efficient and natural way to specify reward functions.

One natural approach is to use pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP [1] and Flamingo [2], to provide reward signals based on natural language. However, prior attempts to use VLMs to provide rewards require extensive fine-tuning of VLMs [3] or complex ad-hoc procedures to extract rewards from VLMs [4]. In this work, we demonstrate that simple techniques for using VLMs as zero-shot language-grounded reward models work well, as long as the chosen underlying model is sufficiently capable. Concretely, we make four key contributions.

First, we propose VLM-RM, a general method for using pre-trained VLMs as a reward model for vision-based RL tasks (Section 3). We propose a concrete implementation that uses CLIP as the VLM and the cos-similarity between the CLIP embedding of the current environment state and a simple language prompt as the reward function. We can optionally regularize the reward model by providing a "baseline prompt" that describes a neutral state of the environment and partially projecting the representations onto the direction between baseline and target prompts when computing the reward.

Second, we validate our method in the standard CartPole and MountainCar RL benchmarks (Section 4.2). We observe high correlation between VLM-RMs and the ground truth rewards of the environments and successfully train policies that solve the tasks using CLIP as a reward model. Furthermore, we find that the quality of CLIP as a reward model improves when the environment is rendered with more realistic textures.

Third, we train a MuJoCo humanoid to learn complex tasks, including raising its arms, sitting in a lotus position, doing the splits, and kneeling (Figure 1; Section 4.3), using a CLIP reward model derived from single sentence text prompts (e.g., "a humanoid robot kneeling").

Fourth, we study how VLM-RMs' performance scales with the size of the VLM, and find that VLM scale is strongly correlated with VLM-RM quality (Section 4.4). In particular, we can only learn the humanoid tasks in Figure 1 with the largest publicly available CLIP model.

Our results indicate that VLMs are powerful zero-shot reward models. While current models such as CLIP have important limitations that persist when used as VLM-RMs, we expect these limitations to be mostly overcome as larger and more capable VLMs become available. Overall, VLM-RMs are likely to let us train models to perform increasingly sophisticated tasks from human-written task descriptions.
